title: How Free Land Made, and Then Unmade, the American Pioneer's Democracy
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

intro.summary: Turner asks what made American society and politics different from Europe's. In 13 essays written between 1893 and 1918, he traces how settlement moved west, drawing on census reports, colonial records, debates and travellers' accounts. He argues that a moving edge of cheap, unclaimed land kept rebuilding society from simple beginnings. That process bred individualism, equality and democracy, and once the free land ran out around 1890, Americans began turning to government to protect the democracy that land had once guaranteed. This is one historian's interpretation, not a tested measurement. He drew on selected evidence, described Native peoples as 'savagery' from the settlers' side, and himself called his first essay a call for investigation rather than a finished case.
background: Through the 1700s and 1800s, settlers of European descent moved west across North America, taking land from Native nations, often by war and treaty.
The US Census mapped a 'frontier line' each decade. In 1890 it announced that no such line could be drawn any more.
In the 1890s, farmers in the West and South formed the Populist movement, demanding government action against railroads, banks and big corporations.
Before Turner, many historians explained American institutions mainly as inheritances from England and older 'Germanic' traditions.
intro.aha: The same free land that made pioneers fiercely individualistic also made them democrats, so when the land ran out, the anti-government pioneer's heirs turned to government regulation to save the democracy that open land had once protected for free.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: In 1893 a young historian read a line in a census bulletin: the country no longer had a frontier line. He thought this quietly marked the end of an era. Most historians looked east, to European roots and the Constitution, to explain America. Turner proposed looking west instead.
primer.quote: The existence of an area of free land, its continuous recession, and the advance of American settlement westward, explain American development.
primer.quote_where: Chapter I, The Significance of the Frontier in American History

primer.heading: What he did
primer.body: Turner followed the edge of settlement from the Atlantic coast in the 1600s to the Great Plains in the 1880s. He used census maps, colonial laws, petitions from frontier towns, debates in Congress and state conventions, and travellers' descriptions. He looked for patterns that repeated at each new edge: who arrived first, how land was handed out, and how frontier regions voted and quarrelled with the older coast.

primer.heading: What he found
primer.body: At every frontier, society started over in simple form. Traders came first, then cattle raisers, then pioneer farmers, then towns. Cheap land meant a worker who was badly treated could leave and start a farm, so rigid classes struggled to form. Frontier regions pushed for wider voting rights, fought coastal elites over fair representation, and sent leaders like Jackson and Lincoln to power. Turner concluded that democracy grew out of these conditions, not out of a written plan.
primer.quote: American democracy was born of no theorist's dream; it was not carried in the Susan Constant to Virginia, nor in the Mayflower to Plymouth. It came out of the American forest, and it gained new strength each time it touched a new frontier.
primer.quote_where: Chapter XI, The West and American Ideals

primer.heading: The twist
primer.body: The pioneer held two ideals: every person free to compete for the land's riches, and rule by the people. While land seemed endless, the two fit together. Once it ran out, free competition produced giant corporations and trusts. Western farmers then gave up some of their dislike of government and demanded regulation, railway control and new forms of popular voting.
primer.quote: Legislation is taking the place of the free lands as the means of preserving the ideal of democracy.
primer.quote_where: Chapter XI, The West and American Ideals

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: Turner's 'frontier thesis' shaped how Americans told their own story for generations, and it still frames debates about inequality and opportunity. It is an argument built from selected cases, not a controlled test. Later historians challenged it for leaving out Native peoples' experience, women, and the role of cities and the East. Turner himself framed his first essay modestly.
primer.quote: This paper will make no attempt to treat the subject exhaustively; its aim is simply to call attention to the frontier as a fertile field for investigation, and to suggest some of the problems which arise in connection with it.
primer.quote_where: Chapter I, The Significance of the Frontier in American History

concepts.title: A frontier is the edge of free land, not a wall
concepts.idea: The American frontier was the moving outer edge of settlement, which the census drew where population density fell below about two people per square mile, and it vanished once settlement became too scattered to draw a single line.

predict.question: Suppose the census had drawn its line at six people per square mile instead of two. In the same year, where would the frontier line fall?
options: Further east, closer to the crowded zone
Further west, deeper into empty land
Nowhere, because only a wall or fort can mark a frontier
why: Right. Moving west, the curve falls from crowded to empty. It reaches six people per square mile before it reaches two, so a stricter cut-off is met sooner, further east.
You might expect a stricter rule to push the line outward. But a higher threshold is reached earlier on the way down the curve, so the line moves east, not west.
The line is not a physical object that stays put. It is defined by the threshold, so changing the threshold moves it.
That is the European idea of a frontier, a fortified boundary. Turner stresses that the American frontier was an edge of thinning settlement, measured by how many people lived on the land.

terms.means: How many people live on each square mile of land
The census's line where settlement thinned to fewer than two people per square mile

model.title: How crowded the land is, travelling west from the Atlantic
model.note: Teaching model: one straight westward path across the continent. A crowded settled zone thins smoothly westward, and three fixed far-western pockets of settlement grow between 1840 and 1880. Only the cut-off of two people per square mile comes from the paper, which takes it from the census reports. Distances, speeds, crowding levels and pocket sizes are illustrative, not census data.

x.label: Miles west of the Atlantic coast

steps.say: This curve shows how many people live on each square mile as you travel west from the Atlantic coast.
The flat line marks two people per square mile. Keep an eye on where the curve drops below it.
This slider sets the year. Watch the crowded part spread west.
This switch adds small pockets of settlement far out west, ahead of the main body.
These boxes report where settlement thins out and how many separate settled areas there are.

explore.prompt: Travel through the century. Find a moment when the edge has gone a long way west but can still be drawn as one line. Then find a moment when no single line can be drawn at all.

goals.text: With the far-western settlements switched on, put the edge of settlement more than 1,000 miles west while there is still only one settled area.
hints: You need two things at once: a lot of distance, and still a single settled area.
Both the main edge and the far-western pockets grow as time passes. You need the edge far enough west before the pockets rise above the two-per-mile line.
Look around the middle of the century and check both boxes as you step one decade at a time.

goals.text: Recreate the census finding that ends the book's story: settlement broken into so many pieces that there are at least three separate settled areas above the two-per-mile line.
hints: Which control adds settlement beyond the main edge?
Switch the scattered settlements on, then slide time forward while you watch the 'Separate settled areas' box.
The pockets need most of the late century to grow past the line.

feedback.correct: Yes. The frontier line is wherever the thinning curve meets the chosen cut-off. A higher cut-off is reached sooner on the way west, so the line moves east. The frontier is a measurement on a gradient, not a built wall.
feedback.incorrect: It helps to picture the frontier as a fixed boundary, but in this account it is the point where settlement thins to a chosen level. Moving west, the curve falls through six people per square mile before it falls to two. So a stricter cut-off puts the line further east.

steps.say: Start in 1790. Settlement is thick near the coast and fades to almost nothing a few hundred miles inland.
The census measured this as population density: people per square mile. Where the curve falls below two per square mile, it drew the frontier line. Here that is about 340 miles in.
Jump to 1820. No wall moved. The whole thinning edge slid west, and the frontier line slid with it.
By 1860 the edge is more than 1,000 miles in. Each census could still draw one frontier line, because settlement thins out only once.
Now add the far-western pockets: gold camps and coastal settlements that leapt ahead of the main edge. The curve now rises back above the line in separate places.
By 1890 the pockets stand well above two per square mile, with empty land between them. The curve crosses the threshold again and again.
With several settled areas there is no single place to draw the line. This is what the census superintendent announced in 1890: there can hardly be said to be a frontier line.

understand.explanation: Turner's American frontier is not a fortified border between two crowded countries. It is the place where settlement thins out into land that is open for the taking. He adopts the census rule: the frontier is the margin where population density falls to about two people per square mile. Decade by decade that margin moved west, past the fall line, the Alleghanies, the Mississippi and the Missouri. The book opens with the 1890 census bulletin, which said isolated pockets of settlement had broken up the unsettled area so much that no single frontier line could be drawn. Turner himself calls the term elastic and widens it to include Indian country. The 'free land' he describes was land taken from Native peoples, as his own references to repeated Indian wars show.
understand.quote: The American frontier is sharply distinguished from the European frontier—a fortified boundary line running through dense populations. The most significant thing about the American frontier is, that it lies at the hither edge of free land. In the census reports it is treated as the margin of that settlement which has a density of two or more to the square mile.
understand.quote_where: Chapter I, The Significance of the Frontier in American History

concepts.recap: The frontier was a moving line where settlement thinned below two people per square mile. When settlement scattered into separate pockets, no single line could be drawn.

concepts.title: Society starts over at every edge
concepts.idea: At each new frontier the same sequence repeated, from trader to rancher to pioneer farmer to settled farmer to town, so American society kept being rebuilt from simple beginnings.

terms.means: A page written over again and again, with the older writing still faintly visible underneath. Turner's image for an old region whose earlier frontier stages still show.
Turner's name for the edge pushed west by fur traders. He also named the rancher's, miner's and farmer's frontiers, each advancing at its own speed.

concepts.recap: Each frontier returned to simple conditions and climbed the same ladder: trader, herder, pioneer farmer, settled farmer, town. American society was rebuilt again and again.

understand.explanation: Turner asks you to stand at Cumberland Gap and watch a procession march west in single file: the buffalo heading for the salt springs, the Indian, the fur-trader and hunter, the cattle-raiser, the pioneer farmer. A century later, at South Pass in the Rockies, the same procession went by again, with wider gaps between its members. Because these types advanced at different speeds, Turner named separate edges: the trader's frontier, the rancher's frontier, the miner's frontier and the farmer's frontier. A settlers' guide from 1837 that he quotes splits the farmer's stage itself into waves: a rough pioneer, then a buyer who clears fields and builds mills and schools, then men of capital who build towns. Each new region went back to simple conditions and rebuilt itself, so an older region's history is a palimpsest, with each earlier stage still showing beneath the present one. This is Turner's interpretation, drawn from travellers' accounts, census maps and local histories, not a measured law. He admits the stages often blurred, overlapped or were skipped, and his scheme treats Indian societies as a primitive 'starting point' rather than as societies with their own histories.
understand.quote: Thus American development has exhibited not merely advance along a single line, but a return to primitive conditions on a continually advancing frontier line, and a new development for that area. American social development has been continually beginning over again on the frontier.
understand.quote_where: Chapter I, 'The Significance of the Frontier in American History'

activities.title: Reading Wisconsin as a palimpsest

steps.text: Start with the oldest layer. Before farmers came, Wisconsin's settlements were fur-trading posts at Green Bay, Prairie du Chien and Milwaukee. French boatmen paddled the rivers to trade with Indian communities, and British influence stayed strong until after the War of 1812.

Next came the lead mines in the southwest corner of the state, which drew miners from Illinois and the South. Turner's account of Wisconsin shows no large cattle-herding stage. Here a miner's frontier fills the place that ranchers took elsewhere, a reminder that the sequence was not identical everywhere.
steps.result: Miner's frontier stands in for the herder

steps.text: After 1832, soldiers who had followed Black Hawk's trail reported rich soil. Settlers from New York and New England came in through Milwaukee and spread across the prairie counties. Turner says Wisconsin was then 'given over to almost exclusive grain-raising.'
steps.result: Pioneer farmers growing a single crop

steps.text: As the soil wore down and land values rose, many native farmers sold or rented their farms, often to German newcomers, and moved into villages. They organised creameries and turned the state toward dairying and mixed farming.
Milwaukee grew from a trading post into a city, and by Turner's day Wisconsin was 'now developing manufacture.' Each of these stages sat on top of the one before.

Turner adds that in his own time North Dakota was at the grain-raising stage Wisconsin had already left behind. The same sequence was running again farther west, starting from simple conditions once more.

activities.takeaway: Read from the top layer down, one state holds the whole procession: trade, extraction, single-crop pioneering, settled farming, then city and industry. Meanwhile the next frontier west was starting the same climb. The stages were real but rough, and Wisconsin had mining where other regions had ranching.

activities.title: Who is this in the procession?
activities.prompt: Each card describes someone Turner, or the 1837 guide he quotes, places on the frontier. Sort each one into its stage.

cards.text: Follows Indian trails up the river valleys, trading goods and guns for furs, often years ahead of anyone who farms.
cards.feedback: Trader. Turner says the trader crossed the continent fastest because Indian communities wanted his guns. He reached each region long before the pioneer farmer.

cards.text: His trading post, set on the site of an Indian village where waterways meet, later grows into a city such as Albany, Detroit or Chicago.
cards.feedback: Trader. The post comes first. Turner traces many later cities to these sites, which shows how the first stage set the pattern for what followed.

cards.text: Drives his herd from range to range and walks it to Charleston to sell, because in a country without roads his product can carry itself to market.
cards.feedback: Rancher. Turner explains that ranching spread fast in remote country because cattle could be driven to market when crops could not be hauled.

cards.text: Keeps 'cow-pens' among the canebrakes and peavine pastures, beyond the edge of the plantations.
cards.feedback: Rancher. Cow-pens beyond the line of plantations are Turner's example of the herder's frontier, which moved ahead of the farmers.

cards.text: Lives in a log cabin beside a dozen acres of girdled trees and corn, does not care whether he ever owns the soil, and moves on when neighbours crowd too close.
cards.feedback: Pioneer farmer. This is the guide's first wave. He farms, but barely, and sells his clearing to the next arrivals before heading west to 'work the same process over.'

cards.text: Feeds his family mainly from the open range and from hunting, using rough farm tools he made himself.
cards.feedback: Pioneer farmer. He still lives off wild resources as much as off crops. That near-primitive way of living is what Turner means by a 'return to primitive conditions.'

cards.text: Buys the land, adds field to field, builds a hewn-log house with glass windows, and helps put up mills, schools and court-houses.
cards.feedback: Settled farmer. This is the guide's second wave. He buys rather than squats, and he builds the institutions of 'plain, frugal, civilized life.'

cards.text: Facing worn-out soil and cheap land farther west, he stays put, gives up single-cropping and turns to intensive, varied farming.
cards.feedback: Settled farmer. Turner says exhausted soil left farmers two choices: move west and keep pioneering, or farm intensively. Staying marks the settled stage, and towns and factories tend to follow.

activities.takeaway: The stages differ in how much each person depends on wild resources and how much he builds to stay. They run from trading with Indian communities, to grazing open land, to rough clearing, to buying and improving. The same ladder was climbed again at every new edge.
hints: Ask what the person lives off: trade goods, herds, rough crops and hunting, or improved fields.
Pioneer and settled farmers both farm. What separates them is whether he plans to stay and build.

concepts.title: Free land as a gate of escape
concepts.idea: Because cheap land lay just west, workers could refuse low wages and subordination by leaving, which kept rigid classes from hardening and pushed society toward equality.

terms.means: Turner's phrase for the open frontier: a way out for anyone pressed by low pay, debt or social rank in the settled East
A release that lets pressure out before it builds into an explosion. Here it means the West drawing off discontented people from the East
A modern label, not Turner's, for the power to walk away from a bad deal. Having it strengthens your bargaining hand

concepts.recap: While cheap land lay west, workers could leave low pay and low rank, so employers bid for labor and no servant class hardened. Turner argues this from testimony, not measurement.

understand.explanation: Picture a worker in an eastern town who is offered low pay and told to know his place. If cheap land lies a few hundred miles west, he can leave and farm for himself, so an employer who wants to keep him must pay more and treat him nearly as an equal. Turner calls this open frontier a 'gate of escape'. Others called it a safety valve, and today we might call it an exit option. Because the gate stayed open generation after generation, no fixed class of servants could set hard, and economic equality fed political equality. Turner builds this argument from period testimony, such as Gallatin and the 1796 land debates. He does not use wage records, and the paper never counts how many workers actually left, so the strength of the effect remains his interpretation.
understand.quote: Whenever social conditions tended to crystallize in the East, whenever capital tended to press upon labor or political restraints to impede the freedom of the mass, there was this gate of escape to the free conditions of the frontier. These free lands promoted individualism, economic equality, freedom to rise, democracy. Men would not accept inferior wages and a permanent position of social subordination when this promised land of freedom and equality was theirs for the taking.
understand.quote_where: Chapter IX, 'Contributions of the West to American Democracy'

activities.question: Visitors to the early United States often noticed that ordinary workers were paid better and bowed less to their employers than workers in Europe did. Before reading on, what is your best guess about why?

options.text: Plenty of cheap land lay to the west, so workers had somewhere else to go.
options.feedback: Keep this guess in mind. The next screens test how far Turner would agree with it and what evidence he offers.

options.text: The U.S. Constitution guaranteed equal rights, so employers could not push workers around.
options.feedback: Many Americans believed this. Turner pushes back: he says the founders' laws mattered less than the conditions people lived in. Watch for that argument.

options.text: American workers had strong trade unions that bargained for them.
options.feedback: Unions grew mostly later. Turner discusses organized labor as a response to conditions after cheap land began to run out, not as the early cause.

options.text: Factories were rare, so there was little demand for wage labor at all.
options.feedback: Factories were fewer than in later decades, but that alone doesn't explain why the workers who did take wages had a strong hand. Something had to make them hard to replace.

activities.prompt: The same worker faces a stingy employer in three different settings. All three come from the paper's own sources. In each case, what can the worker do?

cases.label: Eastern town, land open to the west
cases.text: The employer offers low pay. The worker can pack up, buy cheap land on the frontier and farm for himself. Turner: men 'would not accept inferior wages and a permanent position of social subordination' when land was 'theirs for the taking'. The employer has to raise pay or lose him, and the paper notes that the migration of labor to free lands 'meant that higher wages must be paid to those who remained.'

cases.label: Old World village, no open land
cases.text: Turner describes the peasant and artisan of Europe as 'bound by the chains of social class'. There is nowhere cheap to go, so the worker must take the terms offered. Rank passes down from parent to child, and a fixed lower class persists.

cases.label: The 1796 proposal to limit western land sales
cases.text: In Congress, some Easterners feared cheap land would drain away their labor supply, and they proposed restricting sales. A representative answered that such a law would be 'tantamount to saying that there is some class which must remain here, and by law be obliged to serve the others for such wages as they please to give.' Closing the gate would have recreated the Old World situation by law.

activities.takeaway: What differs between the cases is not the worker's skill or the law of contracts. It is whether he can leave. The open land gives him bargaining power even if he never uses it, and Turner argues this is what kept a permanent servant class from forming.

activities.prompt: Trace Turner's chain of causes from cheap western land to democracy. Click the steps in order along the arrows. Two boxes are tempting detours, so leave them out.
hints: Start where Turner starts: with the land itself, not with any law.
After the worker can leave, ask what the employer is forced to do, and what that does to class lines over generations.
'Eastern industry starved of labor' was a fear raised in the 1796 debates, not Turner's outcome. The Constitution box is the explanation Turner argues against.
activities.explanation: Turner's chain runs: cheap land, then an exit for workers, then higher pay, then no fixed servant class, then economic equality, then political democracy. In his words, 'Economic equality fostered political equality.' The detour to 'Eastern industry starved of labor' records an Eastern fear from the 1796 debates, which the paper reports but does not endorse. The Constitution route is the popular explanation Turner rejects: 'Not the constitution, but free land and an abundance of natural resources open to a fit people, made the democratic type of society in America.' Remember that this is his reasoning from testimony. Each arrow is an argued link, not a measured one.

activities.question: Return to your first guess. In Turner's account, what mainly kept American workers' pay up and stopped rigid classes from forming?

options.text: The option to leave for cheap western land, which forced employers to compete for workers.
options.feedback: Yes. This is the 'gate of escape'. Gallatin made the same point in 1796, tracing the country's happiness 'as much from the great plenty of land in proportion to the inhabitants' as from its institutions. Keep the caveat: Turner argues this from testimony and does not measure how many workers actually went west.

options.text: The equal rights written into the Constitution.
options.feedback: Turner says the reverse. He thinks Americans gave too much credit to a 'glorious Constitution' and that free land did more of the work. Gallatin, writing earlier, gave land at least equal weight with 'the wisdom of their political institutions.'

options.text: Strong trade unions that bargained for higher wages.
options.feedback: In the paper, labor unions rise later, as cheap land is running out, partly to do what the open land had done. Turner treats them as a substitute for the gate, not as its early cause.

options.text: A shortage of factories, so few people worked for wages.
options.feedback: This doesn't explain the bargaining power of those who did work for wages. In Turner's account, that power came from the outside option of free land, not from how many factories existed.

concepts.title: The West grows until it can outvote the coast
concepts.idea: As the Mississippi Valley's share of the population rose from about one-fortieth in 1790 to over one-third by 1840, frontier states with broad voting rights gained the weight to force democratic reforms on the older states.

predict.question: By the 1820s the western parts of New York and Virginia had filled with settlers, while the coast still held the old power. When those two states met to rewrite their constitutions (New York in 1821, Virginia in 1829–30), which way did their voting rules move?
options: Toward more voters, under pressure from their western counties
Toward fewer voters, to protect the coast's property owners
No change, because the federal Constitution fixed who could vote
Voting was handed over to Congress to settle
why: This holds. Turner says western New York forced a wider suffrage in 1821 and western Virginia a more liberal one in 1830, pushed by interior numbers and the threat of losing people west. Virginia's reform was partial: seats stayed unequal.

The coast did try to protect property. Virginia's tidewater argued for exactly that in 1829–30. But the interior's numbers were too large to ignore, so the rules widened, even though the coast kept some advantages.
It is natural to assume a national rule. The 1787 convention actually left House suffrage to each state, which is why every old state had to fight its own reform battle.
Congress never took over state voting rules in this period. The change came inside each state's own convention, driven by its western counties.

terms.means: Handing out seats in a legislature according to how many people live in each place
Every adult man may vote, with no test of property or tax paid
A group big enough that whichever side it joins wins

model.title: How much of the nation lived in the Mississippi Valley?
model.note: Teaching model: four census snapshots only. The shares are the fractions Turner reports in Chapter VI: 1/40 in 1790, 1/7 in 1810, 'over one-fourth' in 1830 and 'more than one-third' in 1840. The last two are drawn at those lower bounds, so the true shares were a little higher. The book gives no figures for 1800 or 1820, so none are shown. Seats and votes are not computed; the step from people to political power is described in words.

steps.say: These bars split the young United States in two. The first bar is the Mississippi Valley, all the land west of the mountains. The second is everyone else.
The grey bar never moves. It marks one quarter of the nation, a yardstick to measure against.
This slider steps through four census years that the book reports. Watch the Valley bar as it moves.
These boxes give the year, the Valley's share, how many people lived there, and how its share compares with 1790.

explore.prompt: Step through the census years and watch when the Valley stops being a sideshow.

goals.text: Find the first census at which the Valley's share of the nation passes one quarter
hints: Which two bars do you need to compare?
Step forward and compare the Valley bar with the grey quarter bar.
It happens before the last year on the slider. Stop at the first year it reaches the grey bar.

feedback.correct: Right. The same pressure that worked on the nation worked inside each old state. Western New York forced a wider suffrage in 1821, and western Virginia compelled a more liberal one in 1830. In Turner's account the old states widened the vote so they would not lose their people to the West.
feedback.incorrect: You may have expected the coast to hold on because it held the power. Turner's point is that numbers plus an exit changed that. The interior counties outgrew the coast, and their people could leave for western states with freer voting rules. New York (1821) and Virginia (1830) both widened the vote, though Virginia still kept unequal seats.

steps.say: 1790. About a hundred thousand people live in the Valley, one-fortieth of the nation. The bar barely shows. Nearly every vote sits on the Atlantic side.
1810. Over a million people, one-seventh of the nation. The Valley's share is already almost six times what it was in 1790.
Seats in the House of Representatives are handed out by head count. That rule is called apportionment: more people, more seats. So this bar is also a rough picture of the Valley's voice in Congress.
1830. The Valley reaches a quarter of the nation, with 3.67 million people. In the next decade Illinois alone gained 318,000 people, while Virginia and the two Carolinas together gained 60,000.

And who voted in those new states? The frontier states entered the Union letting every adult man vote, with no property test. That rule is manhood suffrage. Each new western seat answered to a broad electorate.

1840. Over six million people, more than one-third of the nation. Turner says the Valley now outweighed New England and the South combined in the House and held the balance of power: whichever side it joined won.

So the old states faced a choice. Their own people could move west to freer rules. To keep them, they rewrote their constitutions and widened the vote. Growth on the frontier became reform on the coast.

understand.explanation: The Mississippi Valley's share of the population grew from about one-fortieth in 1790 to over one-third by 1840, using census figures Turner quotes in Chapter VI. Because seats are handed out by population, that growth turned into votes: by 1840 the Valley held the balance of power in the House. The new western states let every adult man vote, so their weight pushed national politics toward democracy, for example in the rise of Jacksonian democracy. They also squeezed the older states, which widened voting to avoid losing people westward; New York in 1821 and Virginia in 1830 are Turner's examples. This is Turner's interpretation built from census numbers and convention debates, not a measured cause-and-effect test. He also credits Revolutionary ideas and city workers, and some reforms stayed partial: Virginia's coast kept unequal seats.
understand.quote: Ohio Valley States, which sprang out of the democracy of the backwoods, and which entered the Union one after the other with manhood suffrage, greatly recruited the effective forces of democracy in the Union. Not only did they add new recruits, but by their competitive pressure for population they forced the older States to break down their historic restraints upon the right of voting, unless they were to lose their people to the freer life of the West.
understand.quote_where: Chapter V, The Ohio Valley in American History

connect.caption: The book has no equation, so this is the model's rule. The blue term is the Valley's share, the length of the first bar. The green term is the Valley's population from Turner's census figures. Because seats follow population, a bigger share means a bigger voice in the House.

concepts.recap: The Valley grew from one-fortieth to over one-third of the nation, and those numbers, voting under broad rules, gave the frontier the weight to push the old states toward democracy.

concepts.title: Two pioneer ideals that could not both survive
concepts.idea: The pioneer's ideal of unrestricted individual competition for resources and his ideal of democracy fit together only while land was abundant. When it ran out, free competition produced trusts and monopoly that threatened equality.

terms.means: Turner's name for the pioneer belief that each person should be free to compete, without limits, for the land, timber and minerals of the continent
A combination of companies brought under one control, large enough to dominate a whole industry
Control of a resource or an industry by one firm or a small group, so others cannot compete on equal terms

concepts.recap: Free competition and democracy were partners only while free land let losers start over. Once the land was gone, competition turned into trusts and monopoly, and the two ideals pulled apart.

understand.explanation: Turner says pioneers held two ideals at once. One was the freedom of each person to compete without limits for land, timber and minerals; he calls this the squatter ideal. The other was democracy: equality, rule by the people, and a hatred of monopoly and special privilege. While free land lay to the west, the two fit together, because whoever lost the race for the best plot could move on and start again, so no winner could lock in a lead. Once the land was taken, the same free competition let the strongest combine into a trust, many companies brought under one control, which could dominate a whole industry and threaten equality. This is Turner's interpretation, set out in essays written between 1893 and 1918, not a statistical test, and he also credits worldwide forces such as steam power and large-scale industry.
understand.quote: But American democracy was based on an abundance of free lands; these were the very conditions that shaped its growth and its fundamental traits. Thus time has revealed that these two ideals of pioneer democracy had elements of mutual hostility and contained the seeds of its dissolution.
understand.quote_where: Chapter XII, "Social Forces in American History" (1910 address)

activities.prompt: Follow the conflict as it comes into view, one stage at a time. Watch what happens to free competition once the land runs out.

stages.label: 1. Land beyond the horizon (before about 1880)
stages.text: Pioneers competed hard for the best bottom lands, timber tracts, salt springs and ore beds. Turner says the West was so free and so vast that the pioneer was hardly conscious any danger to equality could come from this competition. In 1852 Delegate Sibley of Minnesota told Congress that laws punishing lumbermen for cutting government timber should be 'expunged as a disgrace.' Competing freely and being equal seemed to be the same thing.

stages.label: 2. The line disappears (1890)
stages.text: The Superintendent of the Census announced that the frontier line could no longer be drawn. Most of the land that was left was mountain or arid. Turner notes it could only be won with irrigation works, joint effort and capital beyond the reach of a small farmer. The safety valve was closing.

stages.label: 3. Competition becomes combination (1873–1907)
stages.text: Turner traces a chain of business panics. After 1873, separate businesses merged into corporations. After 1893 came pools and trusts, combinations of companies under one control. By the panic of 1907, he writes, it 'seemed not impossible' that free competition would end in monopoly of the most important resources by a small group of men.

stages.label: 4. The giants
stages.text: The United States Steel Corporation was organized with stocks and bonds totalling $1,400,000,000 (Turner's figure) and came to dominate iron mining and steel making. E. H. Harriman drew the railroads into a few great groups and, before he died, hoped to bring them all under his control. Turner's summary: in almost exact proportion as unclaimed resources shrank, combinations of capital grew.

stages.label: 5. Turner's verdict
stages.text: The freedom to compete that once spread opportunity now concentrated it. Turner concludes that the two pioneer ideals had always held 'elements of mutual hostility', and free land had been hiding the conflict. He adds a caveat: these changes were partly the work of worldwide forces of steam and large-scale industry, not only of the closing frontier.

activities.takeaway: Free land kept unlimited competition from producing lasting winners. Once the land was gone, competition produced trusts and monopoly, the very thing the pioneer's democratic ideal opposed.

activities.title: Which ideal is speaking?
activities.prompt: Each card is a pioneer-era claim or practice drawn from Turner's essays. Sort it under the ideal it expresses.

groups.label: Individual freedom to compete (the squatter ideal)

cards.text: Laws punishing lumbermen for cutting public timber should be wiped off the books (Sibley, 1852).
cards.feedback: This puts the individual's right to take resources ahead of any public limit. That is the squatter ideal in its purest form.

cards.text: Among the pioneers, one man was as good as his neighbor.
cards.feedback: This is about equal standing, not about winning a race for resources. It belongs to democracy.

cards.text: A passionate hatred for aristocracy, monopoly and special privilege.
cards.feedback: This is the democratic ideal. Note the word monopoly: it is exactly what unlimited competition later produced, which is where the clash shows.

cards.text: It was 'every one for himself'; honor went to the man whose grasp was strongest.
cards.feedback: This celebrates winning the competition, not equal standing. It is the competitive ideal.

cards.text: New frontier states entered the Union with voting rights for all adult men.
cards.feedback: Broad voting rights are about everyone sharing in government. That is democracy, as the previous concept showed.

cards.text: Restrictive law that prohibits speculation will produce a 'moribund and conservative people' (Harriman).
cards.feedback: Harriman defends unlimited competition and speculation against regulation. He is speaking for the squatter ideal, even as a railroad magnate.

cards.text: The self-made man was the Western ideal, the kind of man anyone might become.
cards.feedback: This is tricky, because 'anyone might become' sounds equal. The self-made man rises by beating others in open competition, so Turner ties it to freedom to rise. It only stays democratic while there is room for everyone to try.

cards.text: Government of the people, by the people and for the people.
cards.feedback: Turner uses Lincoln's phrase as his name for the democratic ideal itself.

activities.takeaway: Both lists were sincerely pioneer. Hold them side by side and the clash appears: the freedom cards allow someone to win big and keep winning, while the democracy cards forbid monopoly and privilege.
hints: Ask whether the claim is about winning a race for resources or about people standing as equals.
Watch for the word 'monopoly' and for anything that pushes back against limits on taking or speculating.

activities.question: According to Turner, why did these two ideals seem to live together peacefully for most of the pioneer era?

options.text: Free land kept opening to the west, so whoever lost out could move on and compete again, and no winner could lock in a permanent lead.
options.feedback: Correct. Abundant land was the hidden condition that made unlimited competition compatible with equality. Turner says the pioneer thought democracy came from political institutions and 'failed to see that it was primarily the result of the free lands'.

options.text: Government regulation kept the competition fair.
options.feedback: Not supported. Turner says that 'to the pioneer government was an evil', and pioneers like Sibley resisted even the land laws. Fair play came from the land supply, not from regulation.

options.text: The pioneers were all equally poor, so competition could never make anyone richer than anyone else.
options.feedback: Not quite. Pioneers did compete, and some won the best bottom lands, mill sites and town sites. Inequality could appear, but it could not harden while fresh land waited further west.

options.text: The two ideals never really conflicted; trusts arose for unrelated reasons.
options.feedback: This contradicts Turner, who says the ideals 'had elements of mutual hostility'. He does admit worldwide forces of steam and industry played a part, but he ties the timing of the trusts to the shrinking supply of unclaimed resources.

hints: Think back to the 'gate of escape' from the earlier concept.
What happened to a pioneer who lost the race for the best land in 1840, and what changed after 1890?

activities.question: Harriman said the country was built by 'magnificent pioneers' and that the trust-builders were carrying on their work. How should we read the captains of industry in Turner's argument?

options.text: As heirs of the pioneers: they carried on the squatter ideal of free competition for resources.
options.feedback: Well supported in part. Turner says the masters of industry 'regard themselves as pioneers under changed conditions', that many rose from pioneer society, and that they applied 'squatter doctrines' to industry. The limit: this reading sees only one of the two ideals and leaves out what their success did to equality.

options.text: As betrayers of the pioneers: monopoly was exactly what pioneer democracy hated.
options.feedback: Partly supported. Pioneers had 'a passionate hatred for aristocracy, monopoly and special privilege', and Turner calls the new concentration a threat to democracy. The limit: Turner does not paint them as villains. He notes Carnegie's democratic ideals and calls them 'the product of these democratic conditions'.

options.text: As both at once: faithful heirs of the competitive ideal, and for that very reason a threat to the democratic one.
options.feedback: This is closest to how Turner frames the conflict. The same freedom that made them is what endangered equality once land was gone. The limit: it is Turner's interpretation, and he left the outcome open. He wrote that it was 'still to be determined' whether they were a menace or 'the most efficient factor' for adapting democratic control.

hints: Ask which of the two ideals each reading keeps in view.
Does Turner judge these men, or does he describe a conflict between ideals that they embody?

concepts.title: When the land ran out, the pioneer turned to government
concepts.idea: Having lost free land as democracy's safeguard, Western farmers dropped their old suspicion of government and demanded regulation, income taxes, railway control and direct popular voting as substitutes.

terms.means: An organized movement of Western farmers after the Civil War that attacked railway rates and pushed for government regulation of them
The 1890s farmers' party, strongest on the prairies, that asked government to own railroads, tax incomes and give voters direct power
Tools of direct voting: citizens propose laws, approve or reject laws, and remove officials, without waiting for legislators
Turner's phrase for society steering economic life through laws and regulation, instead of leaving each person to compete alone

concepts.recap: Free land had protected pioneer democracy for free; once it was gone, the pioneer's heirs made law do the protecting.

understand.explanation: Turner ends on a reversal. The pioneer had treated government as a nuisance: whenever conditions in the East pinched, he could leave for free land in the West, so the land itself protected his equality. Once the 1890 census found no frontier line, his heirs on the prairies faced mortgages, railway rates and trusts with nowhere left to move, so they asked government to do what open land used to do. The Grangers, an organized farmers' movement, pressed for regulation of railway rates. The Populists went further and demanded government-owned railroads, an income tax, and direct voting through the initiative, referendum and recall, which let voters propose laws, approve or reject laws, and remove officials. Turner calls this a shift from individualism to 'social control through regulation by law', made to keep the older ideal of democracy alive. This is his interpretation of party platforms, speeches and voting patterns, not a measured cause, and he names the cost himself: laws that protect democracy also limit the creative, competitive individualism the pioneer prized.
understand.quote: In brief, the defenses of the pioneer democrat began to shift, from free land to legislation, from the ideal of individualism to the ideal of social control through regulation by law.
understand.quote_where: Chapter X, Pioneer Ideals and the State University

activities.prompt: Turner sums up the turn in one sentence: 'The individualism of the Kentucky pioneer of 1796 was giving way to the Populism of the Kansas pioneer of 1896.' Set the two types side by side. Look for what changed, and also for what stayed the same.

cases.label: Kentucky pioneer, 1796
cases.text: He clears his farm with ax and rifle and often squats on land before any title is settled. He sees the tax-gatherer as 'a representative of oppression', and his neighbours' petitions for statehood say that 'a fool can sometimes put on his clothes better than a wise man can do it for him.' He wants government small and local. If the East presses on him, more free land lies just west, and that open land keeps him equal.

cases.label: Kansas Populist, 1896
cases.text: He was usually born in Ohio, Indiana or Illinois, a son of that westward-moving stock. He has pushed onto the dry plains, borrowed Eastern capital and mortgaged his farm, and he depends on railroads to reach a market. Dry seasons and falling prices hit him, and no free land remains to escape to. He demands free silver, government ownership of railroads, an income tax, postal savings banks, farm credit, primary elections, direct election of senators, and the initiative, referendum and recall.

activities.takeaway: The tools flipped, from keeping government away to calling it in. The goal stayed the same: both men wanted a society of equal chances for the common man. The first got it from open land. The second, with the land gone, tried to get it through law.

activities.prompt: Turner says the West's demands on government 'have taken increasing proportions in each region of Western Advance.' Put these steps in the order they rose, from earliest to latest.
items: Pioneers of the early 1800s ask Congress for national aid to roads and canals
After the Civil War, Grangers attack railway rates and seek regulation, while Greenbackers press for more paper money
In the early 1890s, Populists win seats (Kansas, 1891) and demand government ownership of the railroads
In 1896 the Democrats under Bryan take up many Populist principles at the Chicago convention
Around 1910, Roosevelt's 'New Nationalism' demands more federal power to curb monopolies and conserve resources
activities.explanation: Turner traces one line of effort that grows at each step. Early pioneers wanted government help: roads and canals to reach markets. On the prairies the Grangers went further and wanted rules over private railways, and the Greenback movement, by his account, 'grew into' the money demands of the Populists. The Populists then asked government to own the railroads outright and to put power directly into voters' hands. In 1896 a major party adopted much of that program. By 1910 the 'insurgent West' was asking the federal government itself to rein in the trusts. Each step asks more of government, and each comes as free land shrinks.
hints: At each step, ask how much the farmers want government to do: help, regulate, own, or police whole industries.
Turner places national aid to roads and canals in 'the first third of the century', long before the prairies were settled.
Bryan's 1896 campaign adopted ideas the Populists had already raised, so the Populists come before Bryan.

activities.question: Turner's pioneers distrusted government, yet their heirs asked for much more of it. What, in his account, explains the reversal?

options.text: They gave up on democracy and turned to socialism instead.
options.feedback: Turner says the opposite. The pioneer democrat 'had no sympathy with a radical reconstruction of society by the revolution of socialism', and his alliances with organized labor were 'only half-hearted.' The goal stayed democracy. Only the means changed.

options.text: Their goal never changed. Free land had protected equality automatically, and once it was gone they used law to do that protecting.
options.feedback: Yes, and this is the lesson's central point. The same free land that made pioneers fiercely individualistic also made them democrats, because anyone pushed down could leave and start over. When the land ran out, free competition produced trusts, and the anti-government pioneer's heirs turned to regulation to save the democracy that open land had once protected for free. In Turner's words, the Western radical 'must sacrifice his ideal of individualism and free competition in order to maintain his ideal of democracy.'

options.text: European immigrants brought a taste for strong government that replaced the pioneer outlook.
options.feedback: Turner does mention this as a contributing influence: Populist settlers 'mingled in new lands with foreign immigrants accustomed to the vigorous authority of European national governments.' But he finds the movement's leaders mostly among native-born men from the Old Northwest, and his main cause is the end of free land.

options.text: The East had built a strong government, and the West simply copied it.
options.feedback: This reverses Turner's picture. He says these pioneer ideals, 'phrased in the new language of national power, did not meet with the assent of the East.' The push for regulation came from the West against Eastern capital, not in imitation of it.

hints: Ask whether the pioneers' goal changed, or only their tool for reaching it.
Think back to the 'gate of escape': what did free land do for equality when times were hard?
